lines.text: Passwords 101.
Plain text, hashing, salt, rainbow tables, bcrypt, Argon2.
You've seen these words in breach headlines.
But what does a website actually keep when you type your password?
Imagine you sign up for a site with the password sunflower42.
Every time you log in, the site has to check it.
The lazy way is to save it exactly as you typed it.
Plain text.
Then one day the database leaks, and every password is right there.
People reuse passwords, so that leak can unlock their email, their bank, everything.
So a good site doesn't store your password. It stores a hash.
A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length fingerprint.
The same input always gives the same output.
Change one letter, and the whole fingerprint changes.
And there's no practical way to run it backwards.
At login, the site hashes what you typed and compares fingerprints.
It never has to keep your actual password.
Simple.
But there's a problem.
Attackers don't need to reverse a hash. They guess.
Hash a list of common passwords, and look for matches.
Some use giant precomputed tables, called rainbow tables.
And two people with the same password get the same hash. Crack one, and you've cracked both.
That's where salt comes in.
A salt is a random value, unique to each user, mixed in before hashing.
It isn't secret. It's stored right next to the hash.
Now the same password gives a different hash for every user.
Precomputed tables become useless, and each account must be attacked on its own.
The catch? Hashes like SHA-256 were built to be fast.
A single gaming graphics card can test billions of guesses every second.
Salt or no salt, a short or common password still falls in moments.
So why not make the hash slow on purpose?
That's exactly what password hashing algorithms do.
bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2 repeat their work over and over, with a cost you can raise as computers speed up.
scrypt and Argon2 also need lots of memory per guess, which makes graphics-card cracking far more expensive.
For you, a login takes a fraction of a second.
For an attacker, billions of guesses a second become thousands.
But wait. How can you tell if a site does any of this?
Try forgot password.
If they email you your old password, they stored it in a form they can read back.
A properly hashed password can only be reset, never recovered.
Now, your side.
A slow hash buys time. A long, random password turns that time into years.
Use a different one everywhere, and let a password manager remember them.
So here's the complete picture.
Plain text: never.
Hashing makes a one-way fingerprint.
A unique salt per user defeats precomputed tables.
And slow hashes like bcrypt and Argon2 make every guess expensive.
That's passwords 101.
The clever part isn't hiding your password.
It's that a website can check it without ever keeping it.
